Bisector Circle Triad

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and watch three circles that always come out the same size.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Press the buttons to show extra lines and circles, then press Check the claims.
Look for the math

Start with any triangle. Mirror each corner in the two angle bisectors through the other corners, and draw a circle through three of the new points. The surprising part is that the three circles you get are always the same size, however you drag the triangle.

Mirroring a corner

An angle bisector is the line that splits a corner angle in half. The three bisectors of a triangle meet at the incenter L. Reflect A in the bisector through B to get Ab, and in the bisector through C to get Ac; the other four points Ba, Bc, Ca, Cb are made the same way. Press Show reflections to see the mirror lines.

The exact claim

The article states: the circumcircles of A Cb Bc, B Ac Ca and C Ba Ab are congruent. That is confirmed here: all three radii are equal, and they equal the distance from L to the circumcenter O. The logic test checks this at the applet's own start, at right and obtuse triangles and at 2,000 random triangles: it holds every time.

radius(A C_b B_c) = radius(B A_c C_a) = radius(C B_a A_b) = |LO|

Reflect the six mirrored points once more in the other bisector and you get three more circles of that same radius. Press Show small circles to see them; all six circles are congruent, not just three.

Why the sizes match

Each second reflection is a translation: for instance the vector from B to C'a equals the vector from C to B'a. So the triangle O X Y is just a shifted copy of C B'a A'b, and similarly for the other two. Translations keep circumcircles the same size, so it is enough to show that O, X, Y and Z lie on one circle. The bisectors make L the midpoint owner of the relevant segments, which gives LO = LX = LY = LZ: the four points sit on the circle centered at L through O, whose radius is exactly the radius of the three circles.

Where the centers go

The article adds two facts. First, the centers of all six circles lie on the circle centered at L with radius R, the circumradius of ABC; press Show big circles. Second, the lines from A, B and C to the three circle centers meet at a single point on the circumcircle: this is the isogonal conjugate of a point at infinity, drawn when you press Show isogonal point. Both facts hold in the test as well.

One honest caveat: for an exactly equilateral triangle L is O, so the triad circles shrink to points of radius 0, and the old applet's fixed numeric cut-offs stop drawing them. This page hides them there too; move a corner a little and they appear.

Try making a long, thin triangle, then press Show angle bisectors and Show triangles: the circles move a lot, but the three radii stay equal.
